claim: Dynein is the predominant minus-end directed microtubule-based motor that traffics cellular cargoes for many microns at speeds of ~1 µm/s.
source: Dynein is the predominant minus-end directed microtubule-based motor that traffics cellular cargoes for many microns at speeds of ~1 µm/s (Allan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Allan, 2011.

claim: Single molecules of mammalian dynein were at best weakly processive, even in the presence of dynactin.
source: It was therefore surprising when in vitro studies showed that single molecules of mammalian dynein were at best weakly processive, even in the presence of the multi-subunit 1.2 MDa dynactin complex that is needed for most cellular functions of dynein (King and Schroer, 2000; McKenney et al., 2014; Miura et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2006; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012; Wang et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Dynactin is a multi-subunit 1.2 MDa complex that is needed for most cellular functions of dynein.
source: It was therefore surprising when in vitro studies showed that single molecules of mammalian dynein were at best weakly processive, even in the presence of the multi-subunit 1.2 MDa dynactin complex that is needed for most cellular functions of dynein (King and Schroer, 2000; McKenney et al., 2014; Miura et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2006; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012; Wang et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dynein exists in an auto-inhibited state.
source: It was not initially recognized that dynein, like other molecular motors, exists in an auto-inhibited state.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the text and subsequent citations about the phi particle structure.

claim: The AAA+ motor domains of dynein are closely stacked in a structure called the phi particle.
source: One of the first structural studies to investigate dynein auto-inhibition showed that the AAA+ motor domains are closely stacked in a structure called the phi particle (Amos, 1989; Torisawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Coupling multiple dyneins to a DNA origami converted dynein from a diffusive to a weakly processive motor by separating the stacked rings.
source: Several non-physiologic mechanisms of disrupting this interaction, such as coupling multiple dyneins to a DNA origami (Amos, 1989; Torisawa et al., 2014) or binding to a bead (Belyy et al., 2016; King and Schroer, 2000; Mallik et al., 2004; Nicholas et al., 2015), converted dynein from a diffusive to a weakly processive motor by separating the stacked rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using DNA origami.

claim: Binding dynein to a bead converted dynein from a diffusive to a weakly processive motor by separating the stacked rings.
source: Several non-physiologic mechanisms of disrupting this interaction, such as coupling multiple dyneins to a DNA origami (Amos, 1989; Torisawa et al., 2014) or binding to a bead (Belyy et al., 2016; King and Schroer, 2000; Mallik et al., 2004; Nicholas et al., 2015), converted dynein from a diffusive to a weakly processive motor by separating the stacked rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using beads.

claim: An α-helical coiled-coil N-terminal fragment of mammalian BicD2 (BicD2N) couples dynein to dynactin and causes dynein to become highly processive with 5–10 µm run lengths.
source: A major advance in understanding dynein function came from single molecule studies, which showed that an α-helical coiled-coil N-terminal fragment of the mammalian adaptor protein Bicaudal-D2 (BicD2N) couples dynein to dynactin. This causes dynein to become highly processive, with 5–10 µm run lengths, and leads to motor accumulation at the microtubule minus-end (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to single molecule studies.

claim: BicD2N coupling dynein to dynactin leads to motor accumulation at the microtubule minus-end.
source: A major advance in understanding dynein function came from single molecule studies, which showed that an α-helical coiled-coil N-terminal fragment of the mammalian adaptor protein Bicaudal-D2 (BicD2N) couples dynein to dynactin. This causes dynein to become highly processive, with 5–10 µm run lengths, and leads to motor accumulation at the microtubule minus-end (McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to single molecule studies.

claim: Dynein in the activated DD(BicD2N) complex produced 4.3 pN of force.
source: Dynein in the activated DD(BicD2N) complex produced 4.3 pN of force (Belyy et al., 2016), considerably higher than the 0.5–1.5 pN forces reported earlier for dynein alone (Mallik et al., 2004; McKenney et al., 2010; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010; Rai et al., 2013), thus allowing dynein to successfully engage in a tug-of-war with a single kinesin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belyy et al., 2016.

claim: Dynein alone produces 0.5–1.5 pN of force.
source: Dynein in the activated DD(BicD2N) complex produced 4.3 pN of force (Belyy et al., 2016), considerably higher than the 0.5–1.5 pN forces reported earlier for dynein alone (Mallik et al., 2004; McKenney et al., 2010; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010; Rai et al., 2013), thus allowing dynein to successfully engage in a tug-of-war with a single kinesin.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to earlier studies.

claim: The activated DD(BicD2N) complex allows dynein to successfully engage in a tug-of-war with a single kinesin.
source: Dynein in the activated DD(BicD2N) complex produced 4.3 pN of force (Belyy et al., 2016), considerably higher than the 0.5–1.5 pN forces reported earlier for dynein alone (Mallik et al., 2004; McKenney et al., 2010; Ori-McKenney et al., 2010; Rai et al., 2013), thus allowing dynein to successfully engage in a tug-of-war with a single kinesin.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the force measurements cited.

claim: When dynein motor domains are stacked in the phi particle they are locked in a conformation with low affinity for microtubules.
source: Cryo-EM studies showed that when the dynein motor domains are stacked in the phi particle they are locked in a conformation with low affinity for microtubules; disruption of the motor domain self-dimer creates an 'open' state that is still inhibited for motion (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to cryo-EM studies.

claim: Disruption of the dynein motor domain self-dimer creates an 'open' state that is still inhibited for motion.
source: Cryo-EM studies showed that when the dynein motor domains are stacked in the phi particle they are locked in a conformation with low affinity for microtubules; disruption of the motor domain self-dimer creates an 'open' state that is still inhibited for motion (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to cryo-EM studies.

claim: When dynein is bound to dynactin and an adaptor such as BicD2N, the dynein motor domains are aligned in a parallel orientation on the microtubule that correlates with highly processive movement.
source: Only when bound to dynactin and an 'adaptor' such as BicD2N are the dynein motor domains aligned in a parallel orientation on the microtubule that correlates with highly processive movement (Chowdhury et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chowdhury et al., 2015.

claim: BicD2N artificially fused to mitochondria or peroxisome targeting sequences supports robust dynein-driven motility in HeLa cells.
source: Although BicD2N artificially fused to mitochondria or peroxisome targeting sequences supports robust dynein-driven motility in HeLa cells (Hoogenraad et al., 2003), full-length BicD has only a mild effect on organelle re-localization (Hoogenraad et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoogenraad et al., 2003.

claim: Full-length BicD has only a mild effect on organelle re-localization.
source: Although BicD2N artificially fused to mitochondria or peroxisome targeting sequences supports robust dynein-driven motility in HeLa cells (Hoogenraad et al., 2003), full-length BicD has only a mild effect on organelle re-localization (Hoogenraad et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoogenraad et al., 2003.

claim: Full length BicD2 assumes an auto-inhibited conformation that does not bind to or activate dynein-dynactin.
source: It has been assumed that full length BicD2 assumes an auto-inhibited conformation that does not bind to or activate dynein-dynactin.
evidence: This claim is presented as an assumption in the field, supported by inference from prior observations.

claim: BicD2 is composed of three α-helical coiled-coil domains.
source: BicD2 is composed of three α-helical coiled-coil domains; the N-terminal domain (CC1) is involved with dynein-dynactin binding and activation (Urnavicius et al., 2015), whereas the C-terminal domain (CC3) binds adaptor proteins that link dynein to cargo (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The N-terminal domain (CC1) of BicD2 is involved with dynein-dynactin binding and activation.
source: BicD2 is composed of three α-helical coiled-coil domains; the N-terminal domain (CC1) is involved with dynein-dynactin binding and activation (Urnavicius et al., 2015), whereas the C-terminal domain (CC3) binds adaptor proteins that link dynein to cargo (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Urnavicius et al., 2015.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CC3) of BicD2 binds adaptor proteins that link dynein to cargo.
source: BicD2 is composed of three α-helical coiled-coil domains; the N-terminal domain (CC1) is involved with dynein-dynactin binding and activation (Urnavicius et al., 2015), whereas the C-terminal domain (CC3) binds adaptor proteins that link dynein to cargo (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Early yeast-2-hybrid studies showed that the CC1 domain of BicD interacts with the CC3 domain.
source: Early yeast-2-hybrid studies showed that the CC1 domain interacts with the CC3 domain, leading to a model in which BicD forms N- to C-terminal auto-inhibitory interactions (Hoogenraad et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoogenraad et al., 2001.

claim: Early metal-shadowed images of Drosophila BicD suggested interaction of CC3 with CC2.
source: Early metal-shadowed images of Drosophila BicD, in contrast, suggested interaction of CC3 with CC2 (Stuurman et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stuurman et al., 1999.

claim: K10 mRNA is transported by dynein from nurse cells to the Drosophila oocyte during development.
source: During development, K10 mRNA is transported by dynein from nurse cells to the Drosophila oocyte, where it localizes to the anterior margin to establish the dorso-ventral axis of the Drosophila egg (Cheung et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheung et al., 1992.

claim: K10 mRNA localizes to the anterior margin of the Drosophila oocyte to establish the dorso-ventral axis of the Drosophila egg.
source: During development, K10 mRNA is transported by dynein from nurse cells to the Drosophila oocyte, where it localizes to the anterior margin to establish the dorso-ventral axis of the Drosophila egg (Cheung et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheung et al., 1992.

claim: K10 contains a single 44 base-pair transport/localization element (TLS) in its 3'UTR that binds the mRNA-binding adaptor protein Egalitarian (Egl).
source: K10 contains a single 44 base-pair transport/localization element (TLS) in its 3'UTR that binds the mRNA-binding adaptor protein Egalitarian (Egl), which in turn binds to CC3 of Drosophila BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Serano and Cohen, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dienstbier et al., 2009 and Serano and Cohen, 1995.

claim: Egalitarian (Egl) binds to CC3 of Drosophila BicD.
source: K10 contains a single 44 base-pair transport/localization element (TLS) in its 3'UTR that binds the mRNA-binding adaptor protein Egalitarian (Egl), which in turn binds to CC3 of Drosophila BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Serano and Cohen, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dienstbier et al., 2009 and Serano and Cohen, 1995.

claim: Full-length BicD robustly activated dynein-dynactin motility only when both Egl and K10 mRNA cargo were present.
source: Full-length BicD robustly activated dynein-dynactin motility only when both the mRNA binding protein Egalitarian (Egl) and K10 mRNA cargo were present, and electron microscopy showed that both Egl and mRNA were needed to disrupt a looped, auto-inhibited BicD conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both Egl and mRNA were needed to disrupt a looped, auto-inhibited BicD conformation.
source: Full-length BicD robustly activated dynein-dynactin motility only when both the mRNA binding protein Egalitarian (Egl) and K10 mRNA cargo were present, and electron microscopy showed that both Egl and mRNA were needed to disrupt a looped, auto-inhibited BicD conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BicD can recruit two dimeric dyneins.
source: BicD can recruit two dimeric dyneins, resulting in faster speeds and longer runs than with one dynein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complexes with two dyneins move at faster speeds than complexes with one dynein.
source: BicD can recruit two dimeric dyneins, resulting in faster speeds and longer runs than with one dynein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complexes with two dyneins have longer runs than complexes with one dynein.
source: BicD can recruit two dimeric dyneins, resulting in faster speeds and longer runs than with one dynein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Moving complexes predominantly contained two Egl molecules and one K10 mRNA.
source: Moving complexes predominantly contained two Egl molecules and one K10 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-color experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mRNA-bound configuration makes Egl bivalent, likely enhancing its avidity for BicD.
source: This mRNA-bound configuration makes Egl bivalent, likely enhancing its avidity for BicD and thus its ability to disrupt BicD auto-inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and the concept of bivalent binding.

claim: Bivalent Egl enhances its ability to disrupt BicD auto-inhibition.
source: This mRNA-bound configuration makes Egl bivalent, likely enhancing its avidity for BicD and thus its ability to disrupt BicD auto-inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data.

claim: Artificially dimerized Egl activates dynein-dynactin-BicD in the absence of mRNA.
source: Consistent with this idea, artificially dimerized Egl activates dynein-dynactin-BicD in the absence of mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with the Eglzip construct presented in the manuscript.

claim: BicDCC1 showed an ~10 fold enhanced recruitment to microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin compared with full-length BicD.
source: BicDCC1 showed an ~10 fold enhanced recruitment to microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin compared with full-length BicD, similar to the ~13 fold increase observed when mammalian BicD2N was compared with full-length BicD (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from single-molecule pulldown experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mammalian BicD2N showed an ~13 fold increase in recruitment to microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin compared with full-length BicD.
source: BicDCC1 showed an ~10 fold enhanced recruitment to microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin compared with full-length BicD, similar to the ~13 fold increase observed when mammalian BicD2N was compared with full-length BicD (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from single-molecule pulldown experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The truncated versions of Drosophila BicD and mammalian BicD2 behave similarly, suggesting that their mechanism of action is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The truncated versions of Drosophila BicD and mammalian BicD2 thus behave similarly, suggesting that their mechanism of action is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the similar behavior of the two truncated constructs in the experiments.

claim: YFP-BicD forms a parallel coiled-coil dimer.
source: Negatively stained EM images of YFP-BicD show two distinct globular densities at the N-terminus that correspond to YFP, confirming the formation of a parallel coiled-coil dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The most common feature of BicD is a loop formed by parts of all three coiled coil segments.
source: The most common feature of BicD is the loop which appears to be formed by parts of all three coiled coil segments, which is readily seen in averages of all molecules ('global') as well as averages of the most common 'b' orientation molecules (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data and class averages shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distance from YFP to the very bottom of the loop in BicD is 38.7 ± 3.8 nm.
source: The distance from YFP to the very bottom of the loop is 38.7 ± 3.8 nm (± SD, n = 150), in good agreement with Paircoil2 analysis (McDonnell et al., 2006) that predicts the first 258 amino acids of BicD (CC1) to be an α-helical coiled-coil 37.7 nm long (based on 0.146 nm rise/residue).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from electron microscopy images.

claim: Paircoil2 analysis predicts the first 258 amino acids of BicD (CC1) to be an α-helical coiled-coil 37.7 nm long.
source: The distance from YFP to the very bottom of the loop is 38.7 ± 3.8 nm (± SD, n = 150), in good agreement with Paircoil2 analysis (McDonnell et al., 2006) that predicts the first 258 amino acids of BicD (CC1) to be an α-helical coiled-coil 37.7 nm long (based on 0.146 nm rise/residue).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction using Paircoil2 analysis.

claim: The CC1 domain of BicD interacts with a construct containing the CC2-CC3 domains.
source: Pulldowns confirmed that the CC1 domain interacts with a construct containing the CC2-CC3 domains, but not with a construct composed only of CC2 (Figure 2F), consistent with our interpretation of the EM images.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The CC1 domain of BicD does not interact with a construct composed only of CC2.
source: Pulldowns confirmed that the CC1 domain interacts with a construct containing the CC2-CC3 domains, but not with a construct composed only of CC2 (Figure 2F), consistent with our interpretation of the EM images.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The BicD-Egl complex has a remarkably similar overall conformation to that of BicD alone, with the loop remaining intact.
source: Electron microscopy of the co-expressed BicD-Egl complex revealed a remarkably similar overall conformation to that of BicD alone, with the loop remaining intact, and the paired N-terminal YFP domains confirming the BicD parallel coiled-coil (Figure 3A,C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An additional globular structure was often observed adjacent to the loop in the BicD-Egl complex.
source: An additional globular structure was often observed adjacent to the loop (Figure 3A,F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The globular domain observed in BicD-Egl may be the exonuclease homology region of Egl (residues 557–726).
source: The N-terminal region of Egl (amino acids 1–79) binds BicD, and residues 557–726 of Egl contain a globular exonuclease homology region (Dienstbier et al., 2009) that may be the globular structure we observe.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the known structure of Egl and the EM observations, with a citation to Dienstbier et al., 2009.

claim: YFP-BicD no longer retains the auto-inhibited looped conformation in the presence of bound Egl and mRNA (K10min).
source: Electron microscopy of the YFP-BicD-Egl-K10min mRNA complex showed a variety of flexible structures, with the auto-inhibited loop conformation seen for YFP-BicD alone or YFP-BicD-Egl largely absent (Figure 3B vs. Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The presence of K10 mRNA enhanced Egl and BicD colocalization with microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin.
source: The presence of K10 mRNA enhanced Egl and BicD colocalization with microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Both mRNA and Egl are needed for BicD to adopt a conformation that can recruit dynein-dynactin.
source: This observation implies that both mRNA and Egl are needed for BicD to adopt a conformation that can recruit dynein-dynactin.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the single-molecule pulldown data.

claim: mRNPs reconstituted with a mutant K10 mRNA transcript lacking the TLS caused a ~2-fold reduction in the number of BicD-Egl complexes associated with microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin, compared with native K10.
source: mRNPs reconstituted with a mutant K10 mRNA transcript lacking the transport/localization sequence (TLS) caused a ~2-fold reduction in the number of BicD-Egl complexes associated with microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin, compared with native K10 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Egl binds primarily to the TLS zip code but is also able to bind weakly to other regions of the mRNA.
source: This suggests that Egl binds primarily to the TLS zip code but is also able to bind weakly to other regions of the mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data showing reduced but not eliminated binding with K10 mRNA lacking the TLS.

claim: In the absence of either BicD or Egl, minimal movement of labeled K10 mRNA was observed.
source: In the absence of either BicD or Egl, minimal movement of labeled K10 mRNA was observed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by run frequency data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of both BicD and Egl but absence of mRNA, a low-run frequency (20% of maximal) was observed.
source: In the presence of both BicD and Egl but absence of mRNA, a low-run frequency (20% of maximal) was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by run frequency data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inclusion of K10 mRNA enhanced run frequency fivefold.
source: Inclusion of K10 mRNA enhanced run frequency fivefold.
evidence: This claim is supported by run frequency data presented in the manuscript.

claim: K10 mRNA constructs lacking the TLS zip code showed a reduced run frequency (35% of maximal) compared with wild-type K10 transcripts.
source: Similar to the single-molecule pulldowns, K10 mRNA constructs lacking the TLS zip code showed a reduced run frequency (35% of maximal) compared with wild-type K10 transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by run frequency data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mammalian β-actin and S. cerevisiae ASH1 mRNA showed a similar low frequency as K10 mRNA lacking the TLS.
source: A similar low frequency was observed with two heterologous mRNAs, mammalian β-actin and S. cerevisiae ASH1 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by run frequency data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Robust cellular localization of K10 mRNA requires the TLS zip code.
source: Robust cellular localization of K10 mRNA requires the TLS zip code (Bullock and Ish-Horowicz, 2001; Serano and Cohen, 1995), but even non-localizing mRNAs associate with dynein and move bidirectionally in Drosophila embryos (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bullock and Ish-Horowicz, 2001 and Serano and Cohen, 1995.

claim: Even non-localizing mRNAs associate with dynein and move bidirectionally in Drosophila embryos.
source: Robust cellular localization of K10 mRNA requires the TLS zip code (Bullock and Ish-Horowicz, 2001; Serano and Cohen, 1995), but even non-localizing mRNAs associate with dynein and move bidirectionally in Drosophila embryos (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012.

claim: The speed of K10 mRNPs was not significantly different than the minimal DDBCC1 complex (0.42 ± 0.22 μm/s vs. 0.43 ± 0.26 μm/s; p=0.25).
source: The speed of K10 mRNPs was not significantly different than the minimal DDBCC1 complex (0.42 ± 0.22 μm/s, n = 505 vs. 0.43 ± 0.26 μm/s, n = 516; p=0.25, t-test, mean ± SD) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: K10 mRNP run lengths were similar to the minimal DDBCC1 complex (6.4 ± 0.25 μm vs. 5.3 ± 0.17 μm; p=0.8).
source: K10 mRNP run lengths were also similar to the minimal DDBCC1 complex (6.4 ± 0.25 μm, n = 71 vs. 5.3 ± 0.17 μm, n = 66; p=0.8, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: K10 mRNP motility speed was faster than the minimal DD(BicD2N) complex (0.45 ± 0.21 μm/s vs. 0.35 ± 0.19 μm/s, p<0.05).
source: When the fully reconstituted mRNP was independently compared with dynein-dynactin-BicD2N, K10 mRNP motility speed was faster than the minimal DDBCC1 complex (0.45 ± 0.21 μm/s, n = 1126 vs. 0.35 ± 0.19 μm/s, n = 1147, p<0.05, t-test, mean ± SD) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: K10 mRNPs showed longer run lengths than DD(BicD2N) (7.2 ± 0.5 μm vs. 5.4 ± 0.7 μm; p=0.053).
source: Longer run lengths for K10 mRNP were also observed (7.2 ± 0.5 μm, n = 142 vs. 5.4 ± 0.7 μm, n = 137; p=0.053, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The fully reconstituted mRNP is as active as the minimal DDBCC1 or DD(BicD2N) complex.
source: Despite minor differences, all three complexes show long processive runs of ~5–7 µm at speeds of ~0.4 µm/s (Figure 5B–E). On this basis, we conclude that the fully reconstituted mRNP is as active as the minimal DDBCC1 or DD(BicD2N) complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the speed and run length data comparing the three complexes.

claim: 86.7% of motile complexes contained two molecules of Egl.
source: After correction for complexes with two copies of the same color Egl (see Materials and methods), 86.7% percent of complexes were determined to contain two molecules of Egl.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color Egl experiments and stoichiometry calculations.

claim: Speeds of single-colored Egl complexes were better fit to a broad single Gaussian distribution, with a speed of 0.38 ± 0.20 μm/s.
source: Speeds of the single-colored complexes were better fit to a broad single Gaussian distribution, with a speed of 0.38 ± 0.20 μm/s (n = 81) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data from two-color Egl experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Run length distributions of the single-colored Egl runs were significantly shorter than the dual-colored runs (6.4 ± 0.7 μm vs. 12.1 ± 2.4 μm; p=0.045).
source: Run length distributions of the single-colored runs were significantly shorter than the dual-colored runs (6.4 ± 0.7 μm, n = 81 vs.12.1 ± 2.4 μm, n = 62; p=0.045, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data from two-color Egl experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Binding of two Egl molecules favors recruitment of two dimeric dynein motors to the dynactin-BicD-mRNA complex.
source: An explanation that would account for both the enhanced speed and run length is that binding of two Egl molecules favors recruitment of two dimeric dynein motors to the dynactin-BicD-mRNA complex (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the two-color Egl data and citations to recent structural studies.

claim: When two different colored Egl molecules were incubated with unlabeled mRNA, 83% of complexes contained two Egl molecules.
source: In contrast, when two different colored Egl molecules (Qdot-525 and Qdot-565) were incubated with unlabeled mRNA, 83% of complexes contained two Egl molecules, similar to the 87% of moving complexes described above.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from experiments mixing Egl and mRNA on coverslips shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 44% of mRNPs contained two dyneins.
source: Single-molecule pulldowns in the presence of AMP-PNP revealed that after correction for complexes containing two copies of the same color dynein, 44% of mRNPs contained two dyneins (n = 274 dual-colored) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color dynein experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 46% of dynein-dynactin-BicD2N complexes contained two motors.
source: Parallel analysis of dynein (two colors), complexed with dynactin and truncated BicD2N showed that 46% of complexes contained two motors (n = 114 dual-colored).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color dynein experiments.

claim: 50% of dynein-dynactin-Hook1 complexes contained two motors.
source: Finally, we examined the behavior of dynein-dynactin complexes containing Hook1; complexes with Hook3 have been shown to contain predominantly two dyneins (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018). We similarly observed that 50% of the complexes contained two motors (n = 185 dual-colored).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color dynein experiments and comparison to Hook3 data from the literature.

claim: The speed of dual-colored dynein complexes was 0.63 ± 0.26 μm/s.
source: The speed of dual-colored complexes (filled red circles) (0.63 ± 0.26 μm/s, n = 40), were compared to that of single-colored complexes (open red circles) (0.40 ± 0.14 μm/s and 0.74 ± 0.13 μm/s, n = 44).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data from two-color dynein experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Single-colored dynein complexes had speeds of 0.40 ± 0.14 and 0.74 ± 0.13 μm/s.
source: The speed of dual-colored complexes (filled red circles) (0.63 ± 0.26 μm/s, n = 40), were compared to that of single-colored complexes (open red circles) (0.40 ± 0.14 μm/s and 0.74 ± 0.13 μm/s, n = 44).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data from two-color dynein experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The speed of the dual-colored dynein complexes was 58% faster than the single-colored complex slower speed.
source: The speed of the dual-colored complexes was 58% faster than the single-colored complex slower speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from the speed data.

claim: Run lengths of dual-colored dynein runs were 53% longer than the single-colored complexes (8.9 ± 0.5 μm vs. 5.8 ± 1.1 μm; p=0.036).
source: Run lengths of dual-colored runs were 53% longer than the single-colored complexes (8.9 ± 0.5 μm, n = 40, vs. 5.8 ± 1.1 μm, n = 44; p=0.036, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data from two-color dynein experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Recruitment of two dyneins results in an mRNP that moves both faster and longer than an mRNP containing only one dynein.
source: Recruitment of two dyneins thus results in an mRNP that moves both faster and longer than an mRNP containing only one dynein.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the two-color dynein data.

claim: There was no statistical difference in speed between mRNPs reconstituted with WT dynein versus dynein lacking LC8 (p=0.57).
source: We detected no statistical difference in speed between mRNPs reconstituted with WT dynein versus dynein lacking LC8 (0.42 ± 0.13 μm/s and 0.71 ± 0.34 μm/s, n = 396 for WT dynein vs. 0.40 ± 0.13 μm/s and 0.79 ± 0.39 μm/s, n = 488 for dynein without LC8; p=0.57, t-test, mean ±SD) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data comparing WT and LC8-deficient dynein shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The run lengths showed no statistical difference between WT dynein and dynein lacking LC8 (6.2 ± 0.11 μm vs. 6.9 ± 0.14 μm; p=0.46).
source: Likewise, the run lengths showed no statistical difference (6.2 ± 0.11 μm, n = 113 for WT dynein vs. 6.9 ± 0.14 μm, n = 102 for dynein without LC8; p=0.46, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data comparing WT and LC8-deficient dynein shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The putative interaction between Egl and the dynein LC8 light chain does not change the number of dyneins recruited nor does it change the speed or run length of the mRNP.
source: Thus, the putative interaction between Egl and the dynein LC8 light chain does not change the number of dyneins recruited nor does it change the speed or run length of the mRNP.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data comparing WT and LC8-deficient dynein.

claim: After correction for single-colored complexes with two mRNAs, only 11% moving complexes have two mRNAs.
source: After correction for single-colored complexes with two mRNAs, only 11% moving complexes have two mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-color mRNA experiments and stoichiometry calculations.

claim: 89% of motile mRNPs contained one mRNA.
source: After correction for single-colored complexes with two mRNAs, only 11% moving complexes have two mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statement that 11% have two mRNAs, implying 89% have one mRNA.

claim: The observation that each mRNP contains only one mRNA, along with data showing that 87% of motile mRNPS contained 2 Egls, suggests that a previously unidentified function of the mRNA cargo is to ensure recruitment of two Egl molecules to the complex.
source: The observation that each mRNP contains only one mRNA, along with our previous data showing that 87% of motile mRNPS contained 2 Egls, suggests that a previously unidentified function of the mRNA cargo is to ensure recruitment of two Egl molecules to the complex, favoring disruption of the auto-inhibitory structure of the BicD coiled-coil.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the stoichiometry data for mRNA and Egl.

claim: Dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip complexes showed motile properties similar to a fully reconstituted mRNP.
source: Gratifyingly, dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip complexes showed motile properties similar to a fully reconstituted mRNP, and were considerably more motile than control complexes composed of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Egl or dynein-dynactin-BicD, as illustrated by kymographs (Figure 10A).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility data with the Eglzip construct shown in Figure 10.

claim: Speeds of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip were bimodal, with the slower population moving at 0.43 ± 0.21 μm/s and the faster population at 0.95 ± 0.15 μm/s.
source: Speeds of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip were bimodal (blue circles), with the slower population moving at 0.43 ± 0.21 μm/s and the faster population at 0.95 ± 0.15 μm/s (n = 633), whereas speeds of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Egl-K10 mRNA (red circles) were 0.44 ± 0.31 μm/s (n = 560) (p<0.001, t-test, mean ± SD) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by speed distribution data with the Eglzip construct shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Run lengths of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip were longer than those of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Egl-K10 mRNA (7.6 ± 0.03 μm vs. 5.7 ± 0.09 μm, p=0.03).
source: Run lengths of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Eglzip (blue circles) were longer than those of dynein-dynactin-BicD-Egl-K10 mRNA (red circles) (7.6 ± 0.03 μm, n = 84 vs. 5.7 ± 0.09 μm, n = 106, p=0.03, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, mean ± SE) (Figure 9E).
evidence: This claim is supported by run length distribution data with the Eglzip construct shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The reason why mRNA is needed for robust mobility of the reconstituted mRNP is to ensure the presence of the two Egl molecules required to relieve BicD auto-inhibition.
source: In summary, we conclude that the reason why mRNA is needed for robust mobility of the reconstituted mRNP is to ensure the presence of the two Egl molecules required to relieve BicD auto-inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the Eglzip data and the overall experimental results.

claim: A single K10 mRNA can bind two Egl molecules to create a bivalent Egl that efficiently disrupts the BicD loop structure.
source: Single-molecule approaches coupled with electron microscopy suggest that the key to dynein activation is disruption of an auto-inhibited loop structure of BicD. A single K10 mRNA can bind two Egl molecules to create a bivalent Egl that efficiently disrupts the BicD loop structure, freeing CC1 and favoring recruitment of two dynein motors to the complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from EM and single-molecule experiments.

claim: Bivalent Egl frees CC1 and favors recruitment of two dynein motors to the complex.
source: Single-molecule approaches coupled with electron microscopy suggest that the key to dynein activation is disruption of an auto-inhibited loop structure of BicD. A single K10 mRNA can bind two Egl molecules to create a bivalent Egl that efficiently disrupts the BicD loop structure, freeing CC1 and favoring recruitment of two dynein motors to the complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: K10 mRNA cargo orchestrates activation of the motile complex, an elegant mechanism ensuring that only motors properly complexed with cargo can undergo robust motility.
source: K10 mRNA cargo thus orchestrates activation of the motile complex, an elegant mechanism ensuring that only motors properly complexed with cargo can undergo robust motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the overall experimental findings.

claim: The ability of mRNA cargo to orchestrate the activation of the mRNP complex is an elegant way to ensure that only cargo-bound motors are motile.
source: The ability of mRNA cargo to orchestrate the activation of the mRNP (messenger ribonucleotide protein) complex is an elegant way to ensure that only cargo-bound motors are motile.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the overall experimental findings.

claim: Transported mRNAs in Drosophila extracts primarily contain a single mRNA.
source: Consistent with our in vitro studies, transported mRNAs in Drosophila extracts were shown to primarily contain a single mRNA (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012; Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila extracts.

claim: Two Egl molecules may be required to overcome the auto-inhibition of BicD.
source: Thus, two Egl molecules may be required to overcome the auto-inhibition of BicD, and this is enabled by their simultaneous binding to one mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the stoichiometry data and the bivalent binding model.

claim: The requirement for mRNA is biologically important because it ensures that motor activation is coupled to cargo binding, preventing futile dynein activity.
source: The requirement for mRNA is biologically important because it ensures that motor activation is coupled to cargo binding, preventing futile dynein activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental findings and biological reasoning.

claim: In an actomyosin-based mRNA transport system in budding yeast, mRNA was required for processive motion because mRNA stabilized the interaction of two single-headed class V myosins (Myo4/She3) with the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 at physiological ionic strength.
source: We previously showed that in an actomyosin-based mRNA transport system in budding yeast, mRNA was also required for processive motion, but for a different reason: mRNA stabilized the interaction of two single-headed class V myosins (Myo4/She3) with the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 at physiological ionic strength (Sladewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sladewski et al., 2013.

claim: In both the dynein-dynactin-BicD and yeast actomyosin systems, the requirement for mRNA ensures that only cargo-bound motor complexes are motile.
source: Although mechanistically the role of mRNA differs from what we show here with dynein-dynactin and BicD, in both cases the requirement for mRNA ensures that only cargo-bound motor complexes are motile.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from comparing the two systems.

claim: The Rab6GTP and CC1 binding sites on CC3 overlap.
source: A competitive mechanism appears to be the case with Rab6GTP, an adaptor protein that links dynein-dynactin-BicD to vesicular cargo. The Rab6GTP and CC1 binding sites on CC3 overlap (Terawaki et al., 2015), implying that both cannot bind simultaneously.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Terawaki et al., 2015.

claim: Rab6GTP (but not Rab6GDP) in solution or bound to artificial liposomes released BicD2 from an auto-inhibited state to promote processive dynein-dynactin motion.
source: Rab6GTP (but not Rab6GDP) in solution or bound to artificial liposomes released BicD2 from an auto-inhibited state to promote processive dynein-dynactin motion (Huynh and Vale, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huynh and Vale, 2017.

claim: Part of the Drosophila BicD CC3 structure has an unusual feature in which the same residues in the two chains of the coiled-coil adopt different heptad registries, referred to as 'heterotypic' interactions.
source: This possibility is due to an unusual feature of part of the Drosophila BicD CC3 structure, in which the same residues in the two chains of the coiled-coil adopt different heptad registries, referred to as 'heterotypic' interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of BicD structure from the literature.

claim: The heterotypic region of BicD CC3 may act as a molecular switch to promote weakening of the CC3-CC1 interaction following cargo binding.
source: It was proposed that this region may act as a molecular switch to promote weakening of the CC3-CC1 interaction following cargo binding to the adjacent 'homotypic' segment of coiled-coil (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: The function of zip codes in Drosophila appears to differ from that seen in budding yeast, where zip codes in the model mRNA ASH1 are essential for recruitment of myosin motors to the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2.
source: The function of zip codes in Drosophila appears to differ from that seen in budding yeast, where zip codes in the model mRNA ASH1 are essential for recruitment of myosin motors to the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 (Sladewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sladewski et al., 2013 and comparison with the Drosophila data.

claim: Dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex.
source: This result is consistent with recent studies showing that dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018), and that complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force (Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force.
source: This result is consistent with recent studies showing that dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018), and that complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force (Urnavicius et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Urnavicius et al., 2018.

claim: Cryo-EM studies visualized two dimeric dyneins bound to essentially all (>97%) of dynein-dynactin-BicD2N or dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complexes bound to a microtubule in the presence of AMP-PNP.
source: The cryo-EM studies of Grotjahn et al. (2018) visualized two dimeric dyneins bound to essentially all (>97%) of dynein-dynactin-BicD2N or dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complexes bound to a microtubule in the presence of AMP-PNP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grotjahn et al., 2018.

claim: Carter and colleagues found that only 18% of the BicD2N complexes bound two dyneins.
source: Interestingly, Carter and colleagues (Urnavicius et al., 2018) also showed that BicDR1 and Hook3 recruited two dimeric dynein motors, but found that only 18% of the BicD2N complexes bound two dyneins, which they related to the position of the N-terminus of the BicD2N fragment in the complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Urnavicius et al., 2018.

claim: One factor influencing recruitment of the second dynein to Drosophila BicD is the presence of two bound Egls.
source: Our studies with full-length Drosophila BicD suggest that one factor influencing recruitment of two dimeric dynein motors in an mRNP is the presence of two bound Egls, thus establishing a link between cargo binding and full dynein occupancy on dynactin.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data with full-length BicD.
